When agents use this

Before a component becomes golden, and when copied controls change.

Skills: jig-mockup, jig-verify, jig-review.

Golden components is a reference prototype. Native focus containment, screen-reader behaviour and visual acceptance still need a browser and assistive technology.

A real finding: A dialog stole focus on page load

Before: The coordinator found Golden components opening about 5,700 px down, at the dialog’s Close button.

After / recorded fix: The reference has no autofocus attribute. Focus moves to Close only after the person opens the dialog, then returns to its trigger on dismissal.

Why: Focus must follow an action. The regression checks reject load-time focus and require focus after opening.

Source: README.md · Change notes: home and golden components, 8 November 2026

From README.md · Components and their quality bar

Components and their quality bar

Golden examples and components are built on open source parts, not compared alongside them. Where a mature library solves something (menus, dialogs, tabs, inputs, command palette, docking, canvas), the project uses its pick and must not break the library's keyboard, focus and accessibility behaviour. The project's own work is composition and its specific components, which are benchmarked against the closest mature analogues (for example canvas library examples, VS Code panels and tabs, an issue tracker's inbox, a code host's review view).

Every component the project writes meets this checklist before agents copy it, drawn from what mature design systems (Fluent, Radix Themes, shadcn/ui) treat as finished. jig-verify and jig-review check it for interface work.

  • States: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, empty, error, overflow (long titles, long non-Latin text such as Korean).
  • Keyboard: every action reachable; focus visible and never lost or stolen.
  • Accessibility: correct roles and accessible names; tests find it by role and name.
  • Themes: works in every theme the project offers; contrast holds (4.5:1 text, 3:1 controls and focus).
  • Density: readable at realistic data volume, not only sample data.
  • Motion: only to explain a real change, and required wherever something changes on its own (appears, moves, changes state, leaves): without it people miss the change or feel something is off (change blindness; Rensink, O'Regan and Clark 1997), so missing motion needs a disposition: animate eligible changes, but record frequency-gate rejections and reduced-motion stillness (Motion basics below). Reduced motion keeps every fact through labels and receipts. (Person, 7 Nov 2026: "without it a human would notice something.") Motion also replaces words: where a movement shows what happened (slid out of its source, moved into Done, sprouted from its parent), no label narrates it, and the lasting fact lives in structure (links, position, state chips) so it survives reduced motion and a person who looked away (Heer and Robertson 2007).
  • No accidental plain text: interface information uses designed components (state chips with glyphs, type glyphs, structured meta lines, right-aligned muted times), not sentences joined with dots; every action looks and behaves like a control. Plain text is for content the person reads, or is a deliberate choice recorded in the ledger.
  • Icons: drawn from one icon set (SVG, consistent stroke and size), never text characters standing in for icons (a "v" or "⌄" for a chevron renders as a letter in some fonts).
  • Belongs to its host: controls attached to a component (hover or selection actions on a node, card or row) share the host's shape, surface and rhythm: borderless icon buttons in the host's header or a familiar floating toolbar, not a separate boxed widget pasted on a corner. (Person, 7 Nov 2026: node controls that looked like a pasted-on white box with a letter "v" read as "ugly and out of place".)
  • Purpose: carries its ledger ID and passes the ledger check.

From components/README.md · What to copy

What to copy

ComponentUse and contract
ButtonsPrimary for the main action, secondary for alternatives, quiet for attached controls, destructive for deletion. Icon buttons require an accessible name. Compact, standard and coarse sizes use target tokens. Icon plus label is the normal action treatment. Loading keeps a clock and word; busy actions suppress repeat activation.
Chips and badgesInformational status, hugging icon plus word: Ready, Working, Needs you, Complete, Error, Outdated. Outdated has a history icon and dashed edge. These are passive, so have no interactive states; use a button if a person can act.
InputsNative text, textarea, select, checkbox, radio, switch and search. Keep labels, help and associated error text. Selected choices use native checked state. Search has a named clear control that returns focus to the field.
TabsSwitch related panels; roving focus, arrows, Home and End. The selected tab uses the panel surface. The separately labelled state specimens are buttons, not extra tabs in the live tablist.
Segmented controlMutually exclusive view options, exposed as pressed buttons. The live example records the density choice in an output; it does not restyle the state gallery.
PanelTitle, count and one quiet collapse button in the fixed end column. A collapsed strip keeps the identical header. The full title remains available in row details.
List and queue rowsLeading type icon, clamped title, optional meta, status chip. List titles use one line; queue titles use two. Selected rows use a background and edge, with aria-pressed; there is no floating Selected label. Activate to read the full title/path.
Context menuIcon, label, shortcut hint, separator and destructive action. Open the live example by button or context-click. Arrows, Home/End, Escape, Tab and outside pointer dismissal are implemented. The hints are illustrative; global shortcuts are not bound.
TooltipSupplementary detail on hover/focus, with Escape dismissal. The trigger has its own name. The pinned visible specimen shows placement without requiring a hover.
DialogNative modal dialog with a title, description, initial focus and close button. Escape and a backdrop click fade out and return focus to the opener. Closed and closing states are described alongside the open composition; use the live example to exercise them.
ToastPersistent feedback with Undo and a named dismiss button. A durable output records Undo; no timed dismissal. Closing returns focus to Show toast if the person was inside it.
Empty stateExplain the absence and give one useful next action. The standalone creation action is a local receipt, not a data editor.
Scrollbar and dividerThin token-coloured thumb, invisible track, stronger on capable-pointer hover; divider uses the same boundary rhythm.
ProgressFour visual segments plus exact N of M, including complete, loading, error and empty. Loading omits aria-valuenow. Data-mode zero work reads 0 of 0, with an ARIA range of 0–1 and a value of 0 to keep the range ordered.

Each component section states its Craft basics rule and lists its tokens in an expandable disclosure, including shared layout and typography roles. The labelled state specimens use data-state to pin comparison appearances. Do not copy that attribute for hover, active or focus into an application: use native pseudoclasses and real checked/selected/disabled/busy state. Focus specimens remain focusable; disabled examples use the native attribute. An application copying loading markup must also copy the repeated-action guard. Passive components intentionally have no invented hover/disabled/loading states.

From components/README.md · Using the reference in a mockup

Using the reference in a mockup

Copy the appropriate markup, its SVG symbols and the behaviour the mock needs from index.html. Keep the single consistent outline icon set defined there; the simple symbol geometry was authored for this reference. Replace every data-ledger with the mockup's own purpose IDs. Keep labels, ARIA references and unique IDs when copying several instances.

Link stylesheets in this order (adjust paths to the mock's location):

<link rel="stylesheet" href="themes/white-board/theme.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="motion-lab/tokens.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="components/components.css">
<main class="gc">
  <button type="button" class="gc-button gc-button--primary">Save</button>
</main>

Copy typography/type.css along with a theme pack: its import is a shared dependency. Use jig-pages.css for a toolbox document's page chrome, as this reference does. Components use a .gc root; standalone classes such as .gc-button can be composed inside it. Keep component insets smaller than section gaps, use theme semantic roles, and add project-specific components on top. No project-specific cards belong in this folder.

components.css introduces no custom-property definitions or literal colours, lengths, radii, shadows or durations. Zero resets, full extents (100%), grid counts, line clamps and token multipliers express layout rather than new scale values. transparent and currentColor express inherited/absent paint. Motion uses the shared lab duration/easing tokens, all below 300 ms. Only opacity and colour change here; no perpetual loading animation. Hover is gated by both hover and fine-pointer capability. Reduced motion explicitly restores gentle opacity and colour transitions after the theme's blanket reset, with no travel.

Demo / Worst case / Empty / One / Many updates existing text slots, visibility, progress and accessible values. It never inserts markup or writes CSS. Many shows 32 pre-existing rows. Worst case includes a Korean/long title, a long unbreakable path, a billion-item count, exactly 1 item and 0 items, and missing optional metadata. No placeholder dash is inserted for missing fields. Empty and One omit optional metadata too. Inputs and static state specimens keep their own demonstration values; the switch controls the shared item data only.
